lesson.title: Anchors and fast thinking

lead.text: Go back to the jacket. The “was £200” label works as an anchor, a number you meet before you make a judgement, which then pulls the judgement towards itself. Nobody claims £200 is the jacket's real value. It only has to be in front of you when you decide what £120 means.

People have tested this with numbers that were plainly meaningless. Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, two psychologists who spent decades studying how people judge, built a wheel of fortune rigged to stop at either 10 or 65. Volunteers watched it stop, then answered a question with nothing to do with the wheel. They were asked what percentage of the member countries of the United Nations are in Africa.

Each volunteer gave one guess. To compare two groups, line up each group's guesses from lowest to highest and take the one in the middle, the median. A few wild answers cannot drag it far, so it shows the typical guess. A pull from a number that carries no information is called anchoring bias. A gap between two percentages is counted in percentage points.
The wheel stopped at 10 for one group and at 65 for the other. The median guess was 25% after the 10 and 45% after the 65.

lead.text: A gap between the groups shows an anchor at work, but a single gap cannot be compared with other studies. Studies use different anchors, and a gap of 20 means something different when the anchors were 10 apart than when they were 100 apart. What counts is how much of the distance between the anchors turns up in the guesses.

The anchoring index measures that. Take the gap between the two median guesses and divide it by the gap between the two anchors. An index of 0 means the anchors did nothing, because both groups guessed alike. An index of 1 means the guesses moved as far as the anchors, so people simply repeated the number they were shown. Anchors of 0 and 100 with medians of 30 and 50 give 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2.

afterFigure.text: In the wheel study the anchors were 65 − 10 = 55 apart and the medians 45 − 25 = 20 apart, an index of about 0.36. Just over a third of the distance between two random numbers showed up in what people believed about Africa.

lead.text: An anchor is a number someone puts in front of you. Judgement gets a second push from your own memory. Asked how common something is, you rarely count. You check how easily examples come to mind and treat an easy flood of them as a sign that the thing is common.

That shortcut is a heuristic, a rule of thumb that gives a decent answer with little effort. This one is the availability heuristic: judging how common something is by how easily examples come to mind. It works when memorable things really are frequent. It fails when something sticks in memory for another reason. Plane crashes fill the news and car crashes rarely do, so many people think flying is riskier than driving.

Here is a puzzle you can check. Compare English words that start with k with English words that have k as the third letter. Most people say the first kind is more common. Searching memory by a word's first letter is far easier than by its third, so words like “king” and “kettle” arrive at once while “ask” and “like” hardly come up. Words with k third are about twice as common.
A sample of 600 English words that contain k gives a way to check the guess most people make.

steps.headline: A quick answer and a slow check

lead.text: A third shortcut is the simplest: the first answer that pops into your head. Following Kahneman, psychologists call fast, effortless thinking System 1, and the slower, deliberate checking that can follow it System 2. These are names for two ways of thinking and do not match two organs in the brain. You move between them all day.

System 1 is usually right, which is why it is in charge. It lets you catch a ball or read a face without a calculation. The trouble comes with a problem that looks easy and is not, because System 1 hands over its answer so smoothly that nothing prompts a check. Try a small one. A cap and a scarf cost £6 together, and the scarf costs £4 more than the cap. The answer that springs to mind is that the cap costs £2. Put it back into the problem: a £2 cap makes the scarf £6, and the pair cost £8.

To solve it properly, call the cap's price x. The scarf is x + 4, so together they cost 2x + 4 = 6, which gives x = 1. The cap costs £1. The habit to keep is putting the quick answer back into the problem and seeing whether the total still works. It takes a few seconds, and it is worth doing when a wrong answer would be expensive.
A bat and a ball cost £1.10 together. The bat costs £1.00 more than the ball. Notice the first answer that comes to mind, then check it against the total.

lesson.orientation: Measure the pull of an anchor and the bias of availability, then check a fast intuition with a slow one.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two shops sell the same jacket for £120. In the first, the label reads “was £200, now £120”. In the second, £120 is the only price on the label. Most people say the first jacket feels like the better deal, though the cloth, the stitching and the money leaving your pocket are the same.

The £200 told you nothing true about the jacket. It was simply the first number you saw, and your sense of what £120 means was measured from it. Quick judgement works like this a good deal of the time. What you meet first, and what comes to mind most easily, quietly shapes the answer you give.

This lesson follows one afternoon of snap judgements, from a price tag to a worry that a news story planted and on to a sum done in your head at the till. Each stop shows a shortcut at work and how far it can pull a guess.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure how far a starting number pulls an estimate, and spot when a quick answer deserves a check.

recap.keyIdea: The first number you meet pulls your estimate, and what comes to mind easily feels common. Fast intuition is often right, so the skill is checking it when the stakes call for it.

blocks.text: You found that a random wheel moved median estimates by 20 points, an anchoring index of 0.4 for the tree ages, and that only a third of k-words start with k. The bat and ball cost 5p, not the 10p that springs to mind.

recap.nextHook: The numbers and stories in front of you bend a quick judgement. So do the people beside you. The next lesson starts on a station platform, where a stranger collapses and everyone nearby has to decide what to do.

questions.prompt: After several news reports of shark attacks, a swimmer judges sharks a bigger risk than drowning. Judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind is which heuristic?
hints: The examples are readily available in memory.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The availability heuristic: vivid, easily recalled cases feel common.

questions.onCorrect: Vivid, easily recalled cases feel common. That is the availability heuristic.

misconceptions.feedback: Anchoring is the pull of a starting number. This is about how easily examples come to mind.

questions.prompt: A pen and a notebook cost £2.20 together. The notebook costs £2.00 more than the pen. How much does the pen cost, in pence?
hints: Write the notebook's price in terms of the pen's.
The two prices add to 220p.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Pen x, notebook x + 200: 2x + 200 = 220, so x = 10p.

questions.onCorrect: Check the quick answer against the total: the pen is 10p and the notebook £2.10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the answer that springs to mind. Check it: the notebook would then cost £2.20 alone.
That is the total of both. The pen is only part of it.

The denominator is 600.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 200/600 = 0.333, or 33.3%: words with k third are twice as common, though harder to recall.

citations.claim: An anchor is a number met before a judgement that pulls the judgement towards itself. Tversky and Kahneman's rigged wheel stopped at 10 or 65 before volunteers estimated the share of UN members that are African countries. The median is the middle guess. Anchoring bias is the pull of a starting number that carries no information.
After the wheel stopped on 10 the median estimate was 25%, and after 65 it was 45%, a gap of 20 percentage points from a plainly irrelevant number.

The anchoring index is the gap between median estimates divided by the gap between anchors. 0 means the anchors were ignored and 1 means estimates moved as far as the anchors. Anchors 0 and 100 with medians 30 and 50 give 0.2. The wheel study gives 20 ÷ 55, about 0.36.
Anchors of 10 and 70 with medians of 30 and 51 give an anchoring index of 21 ÷ 60 = 0.35.
Anchors of 20 and 80 with median oak-age estimates of 35 and 59 years give an index of 24 ÷ 60 = 0.4.

The availability heuristic judges how common something is by how easily examples come to mind. It misleads when memorable events are not frequent. Words with k as the third letter are about twice as common as words starting with k.
In a sample of 600 words containing k, 200 start with k, which is 33.3%; words with k third are twice as common though harder to recall.

Kahneman's System 1 is fast, effortless thinking and System 2 is slower, deliberate checking; they are names for ways of thinking, not brain organs. A quick answer to a cap-and-scarf style problem can fail a check that sets up 2x + 4 = 6.
A bat and a ball cost £1.10 and the bat costs £1.00 more. The quick answer of 10p would make the total £1.20, and the ball costs 5p.
Anchors of 100 and 500 produce median estimates of 220 and 340. What is the anchoring index? (340 − 220)/(500 − 100) = 120/400 = 0.3.
